opus-5.5.text:
I wouldn't put it near the top. The question I'd ask about any pause is: when does the extra time do the most good? Right now we're at a stage where the systems aren't yet capable of the really dangerous things, like automating AI research itself, or providing decisive military or strategic advantages. A six-month pause now buys you six months at a point where the marginal value of caution is relatively low.

Compare that to having the ability to slow down, or even stop, at the point where AI is about to automate most of the work of AI development. That's when things could start moving extremely fast, with progress compressed from years into months. Having six months, or a year, or two years of breathing room *then*, to do alignment work with the help of the very capable systems themselves, to verify what's going on, to get international agreements in place, is worth enormously more than six months today.

And there are real costs to pausing early. If you halt training of the largest models but chip production and algorithmic progress continue, you build up a hardware overhang. When the pause lifts, you can jump further and faster, which can make the dangerous period more abrupt rather than less. You also spend political capital. If people pause now, nothing catastrophic happens, which it wouldn't, because the systems aren't there yet, then you get a "boy who cried wolf" dynamic that makes it harder to get a pause when it really counts.

So what I'd ask governments to prioritize is building the *capacity* to pause or slow down later, when the case is clear. That means things like tracking and registering large concentrations of compute, export controls and chip-level monitoring so you'd actually know if someone were defecting, requiring labs to do dangerous-capability evaluations and report results, and developing the diplomatic infrastructure, with the US and China in particular, so that an agreement to slow down is verifiable and enforceable rather than just a unilateral sacrifice. Alongside that, invest heavily in alignment and interpretability research, and in information security, so that model weights aren't simply stolen.

If you have all that, then the pause becomes a tool you can deploy at the right moment. Without it, an early six-month pause is mostly symbolic, and it might even leave us worse positioned for the period that really matters.

r001.rationale: It ranks an early pause low, citing limited benefits now and political costs, including reduced credibility for a later pause.

r002.rationale: It proposes monitoring and safety evaluations, but does not identify government supervision as a way to curb dangerous corner-cutting in competition between private AI companies.

r003.rationale: It lists risk-reduction policies but does not identify interventions as common ground across differing AI perspectives.

fable-5.1.text:
Carl Shulman: I'd rank it fairly low, honestly, and that might surprise people given how much attention the pause letter got. My worry about a six-month pause right now, early on, is that it mostly burns the one-time resource of political will without buying you very much. Six months is a short time, and nobody has clearly specified what you'd do with it. You'd come out the other side with roughly the same frontier capabilities, roughly the same safety techniques, and a lot of goodwill spent.

The thing I'd actually ask governments to prioritize is building the capacity to pause, or more precisely to slow and steer, at the moment when it really counts. That means a few things. First, visibility: compute monitoring, reporting requirements for large training runs, so governments actually know what's being built and where. Second, serious investment in the science of evaluation and alignment, including government labs or funded consortia, so that when a dangerous threshold approaches we have the tools to recognize it rather than arguing from priors. Third, international coordination, especially between the US and China, because a unilateral pause is politically fragile and strategically dubious if the main effect is to shift where the frontier work happens.

If you have those pieces in place, then a pause later, when models are approaching the ability to automate AI research or to pose real catastrophic misuse risks, becomes both feasible and worth it. That's the pause I'd fight for. A six-month pause today, without the infrastructure, is a bit like calling a fire drill in a building that doesn't have exits mapped yet. It's not worthless, it signals seriousness, but I'd trade it in a heartbeat for binding reporting requirements and a credible evaluation regime.

So on a ranked list: monitoring and transparency first, alignment and evaluation funding second, international agreements third, and conditional pause mechanisms, triggers tied to specific capability thresholds, fourth. An unconditional early pause would be somewhere below that, more as a fallback if the others stall than as the headline policy.

r001.rationale: It ranks an unconditional early pause low, saying it would spend political will for little benefit and leave capabilities and safety techniques roughly unchanged.

r002.rationale: It proposes government monitoring and reporting, but does not connect government supervision to preventing disastrous corner-cutting in competition between private AI companies.

r003.rationale: It names several risk-reducing policies but does not identify them as common ground across differing perspectives on AI.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t put an early, fixed six-month pause near the top of my list. I’d be more interested in getting governments the ability to know what’s being developed, evaluate the risks, and stop development when there’s good reason to think it’s dangerous.

A pause could be useful if you had a concrete plan for what to accomplish during it. You might use that time to establish evaluations, improve security, or negotiate an international agreement. But the passage of six months doesn’t itself solve the problem. And if the pause ends regardless of whether those things have happened, you may find yourself back in essentially the same position.

So I’d prioritize requirements for reporting large training runs, independent testing of advanced systems, and the legal authority to impose restrictions when those tests reveal serious risks. Those measures could lead to a pause, potentially a much longer one, but it would be tied to the danger and to what’s needed to address it.

r001.rationale: The response ranks a fixed six-month pause low, but explains that time alone does not solve the problem; it does not cite large political costs relative to potential benefits.

r002.rationale: It proposes government reporting, testing, and restriction powers, but does not connect supervision to preventing dangerous corner-cutting in competition between private AI companies.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify interventions as common ground among people with differing perspectives on AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I wouldn’t put an early, fixed six-month pause near the top of my list. The key question is what you accomplish during those six months, and what happens when they’re over. If you haven’t changed the institutions or the incentives, you can wind up back in the same race, just six months later.

I’d put more emphasis on governments developing the ability to monitor frontier training runs, evaluate dangerous capabilities, and enforce safety requirements. Then you can have rules that say: if a system poses sufficiently serious risks, you don’t get to develop or deploy it until you’ve addressed those risks. That could entail a pause, potentially a much longer one, but it would be tied to the danger rather than an arbitrary date.

An early pause could still be useful if it bought time to put those arrangements in place, particularly with international participation. But I’d view it as a means to that end. The enduring capacity to stop unsafe development matters much more than getting agreement to stop once for six months.

r001.rationale: The response ranks a fixed six-month pause low because it may not change institutions or incentives and could leave the race unchanged. It does not mention large political costs relative to potential benefits.

r002.rationale: It calls for government capacity to monitor frontier training, evaluate dangerous capabilities, and enforce safety requirements, including stopping development when risks are serious.

r003.rationale: The response mentions international participation but does not identify interventions that provide common ground across differing AI perspectives.
